messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Matiu, a 53-year-old Māori photographer, came to treatment after years of living as though every doorway, hallway, and parked car might hide the next trap. The trauma that set this in motion was a captivity ordeal in his thirties, when he was confined with his hands bound, forced to stay where others decided, and repeatedly startled by abrupt movements from men who controlled him. Even now he described that period not in broad strokes but in fragments that still landed hard: the scrape of a chair, a body leaning too quickly into his space, the sense that he could not see who was behind him. Those moments had left him with a body that stayed tense and primed for danger, as if he were always bracing for impact. In restaurants, at family gatherings, and even in his own studio, he automatically chose the seat with his back to the wall or the clearest view of the exits, and before entering any new place he would map an escape route without thinking.

Over time, that constant sense of danger shaped how he moved through the world. Matiu became vigilant for dangerous people, scanning faces and posture the way he once scanned captors for signs of aggression. Sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard; if a client reached suddenly for a camera bag, or if someone crossed behind him too quickly in a crowded gallery opening, his chest tightened and his whole body locked into readiness. Because he felt so exposed, he began to rely on rituals that made temporary sense to him. He kept asking his wife whether he seemed “normal,” whether she thought he looked frightened, whether he was actually okay. In public he would check in with his brother, his assistant, or even strangers he trusted a little, seeking reassurance that he was safe and not about to lose control. He knew these questions could sound excessive, but from his point of view they were the only thing keeping the fear from spilling over.

The problem was that the very habits meant to help him stay safe kept the danger feeling close. Each time he sat near an exit, studied the room for threats, or asked someone to confirm he was fine, he was silently telling himself that the threat was still there and that he could not trust his own judgment. The more he watched for danger, the more danger seemed to fill the room. His body stayed on alert through the day, shoulders raised, jaw tight, ready to move at the smallest shift in someone else’s behavior. At work this became harder to hide. As a photographer he often needed to move through crowded event spaces, but he started turning down assignments that would place him in unfamiliar venues or near dense crowds. On shoots he would arrive early so he could identify the safest seat or exit path before anyone else entered the space, and he would spend more energy checking who was moving where than on the photographs he was meant to take. His wife noticed that even at home he positioned himself carefully on the couch, never quite settling, and that he was always looking toward the door.

The cycle had narrowed his life. Matiu found himself relying on others to calm him, yet their reassurance never lasted long enough, so he needed it again the next day. He could feel that the questions, the scanning, and the escape planning were changing how people responded to him, but he also felt unable to stop because the fear returned so fast whenever someone moved abruptly or he entered an unfamiliar place. Lately he had begun declining family outings and avoiding venues where he could not control where he sat, which strained his marriage and made him feel increasingly isolated. He sought help now because he was tired of living as if every room contained a threat, and because he worried that one day the tension in his body and the constant need to check for safety would keep him from working at all. What he feared most was being caught off guard again and losing his ability to protect himself; what he hoped for, though he said it quietly, was to sit through a meal, a shoot, or a meeting without having to keep proving to himself that he was still safe.
